question.text: Is laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery feasible?
question.context: Laparoscopic techniques can be used to treat patients whose antireflux surgery has failed. Case series. Two academic medical centers. Forty-six consecutive patients, of whom 21 were male and 25 were female (mean age, 55.6 years; range, 15-80 years). Previous antireflux procedures were laparoscopic (21 patients), laparotomy (21 patients), thoracotomy (3 patients), and thoracoscopy (1 patient). The cause of failure, operative and postoperative morbidity, and the level of follow-up satisfaction were determined for all patients. The causes of failure were hiatal herniation (31 patients [67%]), fundoplication breakdown (20 patients [43%]), fundoplication slippage (9 patients [20%]), tight fundoplication (5 patients [11%]), misdiagnosed achalasia (2 patients [4%]), and displaced Angelchik prosthesis (2 patients [4%]). Twenty-two patients (48%) had more than 1 cause. Laparoscopic reoperative procedures were Nissen fundoplication (n = 22), Toupet fundoplication (n = 13), paraesophageal hernia repair (n = 4), Dor procedure (n = 2), Angelchik prosthesis removal (n = 2), Heller myotomy (n = 2), and the takedown of a wrap (n = 1). In addition, 18 patients required crural repair and 13 required paraesophageal hernia repair. The mean +/- SEM duration of surgery was 3.5+/-1.1 hours. Operative complications were fundus tear (n = 8), significant bleeding (n = 4), bougie perforation (n = 1), small bowel enterotomy (n = 1), and tension pneumothorax (n = 1). The conversion rate (from laparoscopic to an open procedure) was 20% overall (9 patients) but 0% in the last 10 patients. Mortality was 0%. The mean +/- SEM hospital stay was 2.3+/-0.9 days for operations completed laparoscopically. Follow-up was possible in 35 patients (76%) at 17.2+/-11.8 months. The well-being score (1 best; 10, worst) was 8.6+/-2.1 before and 2.9+/-2.4 after surgery (P<.001). Thirty-one (89%) of 35 patients were satisfied with their decision to have reoperation.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The case describes a series of laparoscopic reoperations for failed antireflux surgery. The data indicates a high success rate with laparoscopic reoperation, with a low conversion rate to open procedures and no mortality. The patients reported high levels of satisfaction with the reoperation. Therefore, laparoscopic reoperation is feasible.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The low conversion rate (20%) from laparoscopic to open procedures and the high patient satisfaction (89% satisfied) strongly support the feasibility of laparoscopic reoperation.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other surgical approaches might be considered, the case specifically focuses on laparoscopic reoperation. The data presented demonstrates its effectiveness and safety, making it the most appropriate answer.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The case series demonstrates that laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery is feasible, with a low conversion rate (20%) and no mortality. The majority of patients had successful outcomes with manageable complications.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The 0% conversion rate in the last 10 patients and 0% mortality rate indicate high feasibility
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered open conversion as alternative, but laparoscopic approach showed superior safety and efficacy in this series

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The case presents a series of 46 patients who underwent laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery with a 0% mortality rate, 20% conversion rate, and high patient satisfaction (89% satisfied). The feasibility is supported by technical success and acceptable morbidity, especially with recent improvements (0% conversion in last 10 patients).
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 0% mortality and 89% patient satisfaction with laparoscopic reoperation in 35 follow-up patients.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Open conversion was possible in 20% of cases, but recent data show no conversions in the last 10, suggesting improved technique; no contraindications to laparoscopy were reported, and outcomes are favorable.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Low conversion rate (20%) in the last 10 patients, with no mortality and high patient satisfaction.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other surgical approaches (e.g the need for open surgery due to severe complications) could be considered, but the reported success and low complication rates for laparoscopic redo procedures argue against the necessity of open surgery and support feasibility of laparoscopic reoperation.
